value.overview: The Black Swift is a large, dark swift that spends most of its life in the air, catching flying insects over mountains, forests, valleys, and coastal areas. It is an uncommon and locally distributed species with scattered breeding sites. Nests are usually placed on protected cliffs, often behind waterfalls or in damp recesses. The species is difficult to study because it forages high overhead and uses remote nesting locations. In Costa Rica, it is mainly encountered during migration.
value.classification: The Black Swift belongs to the swift family Apodidae and the order Apodiformes. Its scientific name is Cypseloides niger.
value.identification: This is a large, long-winged swift with an almost entirely blackish body, long pointed wings, and a slightly notched tail. Pale edging or faint whitish scaling may be visible on the forehead and underparts, especially in immature birds. It often flies with steady, relatively slow wingbeats compared with smaller swifts, interspersed with gliding and soaring. Birds are commonly seen singly or in small groups, usually high above the ground, and may give quiet, high-pitched chattering notes.
value.rangeHabitat: The Black Swift breeds in scattered locations from western Canada through the western United States and Mexico, with additional populations in parts of the Caribbean and Central America. It uses steep mountain cliffs, sea cliffs, canyons, and rocky stream valleys, especially sites near waterfalls or other sheltered, damp surfaces. It forages widely over forests, open country, and mountain slopes. In Costa Rica, it is a very uncommon migrant or seasonal visitor, generally reported in suitable mountainous or aerial-foraging habitat rather than as a widespread resident.
value.migrationStatus: The Black Swift is migratory in much of North America. Birds breeding in Canada, the United States, and northern Mexico move south after breeding, with wintering areas extending through Central America into northern South America. In Costa Rica, it occurs mainly during migration and is not generally considered a regular breeding resident; sightings are uncommon and may be localized or irregular.
value.breeding: Black Swifts usually nest on inaccessible vertical cliffs, in caves, sea caves, or behind waterfalls where spray and shade provide protection from predators and weather. The nest is a small cup made from mud, moss, ferns, and other plant material, and may be reused. A pair normally raises one chick per season. Both adults incubate the single white egg and feed the nestling by regurgitating a mixture of insects and saliva. The young remain in the nest until capable of sustained flight.
value.dietFeeding: The Black Swift feeds almost entirely while flying. Its prey includes flies, beetles, wasps, mayflies, caddisflies, winged ants, termites, and other aerial insects; spiders may also be taken. It may forage alone or in small flocks and can travel widely from nesting or roosting sites. Birds often feed high above forests and mountains, but cloudy weather, insect emergences, or local air currents may bring them closer to the ground.
value.behavior: This swift is highly aerial and spends much of the day flying, gliding, and wheeling over broad areas. It is usually quiet compared with many other swifts and can be difficult to detect except when silhouetted against the sky. Black Swifts roost and nest in protected cliff sites, sometimes in small colonies. Courtship may involve prolonged aerial chases, and the species is strongly associated with remote, predator-resistant locations that are often difficult for people to access.

conservation.populationTrend: Declining. Long-term monitoring and regional studies indicate marked decreases in abundance, with especially serious concern for breeding populations in western North America.
conservation.threats: Important concerns include loss or disturbance of waterfall and cliff nesting sites, changes in water flow and drought that can affect damp nesting locations, declines in aerial insect prey, pesticides, severe weather, and climate change. Because Black Swifts migrate across many countries, threats may occur on both breeding and wintering grounds. Poor knowledge of migration routes and winter distribution also complicates conservation planning.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect waterfalls, sea cliffs, canyon walls, and surrounding forests used for nesting and roosting, while minimizing disturbance during the breeding season. Maintain natural stream flows and watershed health, reduce unnecessary insecticide use, and conserve habitats along migration routes. Support long-term monitoring through responsible bird observations and reporting, especially in Costa Rica and other migration areas where the species is uncommon and easily overlooked.
